note: Promotion to the tracked schema (roadmap Phase 1 backfill). Track groups follow the (XX) prefixes already embedded in the source theme names; only empty fields are filled.

themes.description: Tracing your own water back — river, well, tank or main — and who keeps it safe along the way.
The path of used water from your drain — sewer, septic or ground — and your household's end of that bargain.

themes.theme: When the water is not safe (WA)
themes.description: The signs and notices of unsafe water, and the boil, filter and treat options ranked by what they remove.
Moving and storing water without contaminating it — clean containers, covered storage and the ladle rule.
Flooding where you live — where it comes from, what it touches first, and the household moves before and after.
Drought and scarcity — rationing a household honestly, and the uses that go first.
The simple tests and observations that say something real about water, and reading an official quality report.
Finding a leak with the meter-still test, the repairs within reach, and what a slow drip costs over a year.
What water costs where you live — the bill, the tariff, the subsidy — and using the price to find the waste.
Wells, standpipes and irrigation shared by many — the rules, rotas and disputes of a common source.

themes.theme: What this ground is made of (LD)
themes.description: Reading your local soil and rock — what drains, what slips, what grows — from a hole you dug yourself.

themes.theme: Who owns the ground you stand on (LD)
themes.description: Titles, tenancies and commons — the ownership map of your own area and where it is recorded.
Erosion and degradation — the signs of ground leaving, and the plantings and barriers that hold it.
Preparing a bed, choosing what suits the soil and season, and tending one deliberate crop to harvest.
Vacant lots and margins — who actually owns them, and the lawful routes to putting them to use.
Making a real map of a real place — boundaries, water, slopes, uses — accurate enough for someone else to follow.
The land rules that bind where you live — zoning, building, clearing — and where a decision can be looked up.
Taking one degraded patch back — clearing, soil, planting, protection — and keeping it alive past the first season.
Surveying the species of one real place, and what their presence or absence says about its health.
Sealed ground, drains and heat — what paving does to water and temperature, and the green that repairs it.
Collecting older residents' accounts of past seasons and comparing them honestly to the record.
A simple weather log kept properly — instrument, time, place — until it becomes data.
Extreme heat where you live — who it endangers, the hours that matter, and cooling a body and a room.
Cold snaps — the household risks from pipes to lungs, and protecting the people heating one room.
Shifting rains and growing seasons — reading the change in local planting, prices and water.
The storms your region actually gets, their warning signs, and the before-during-after sequence for a household.
What is in the air you breathe — smoke, dust, exhaust — reading an air quality index and acting on a bad day.
Probability, timing and range in a real forecast — what it promises, what it cannot, and planning with it.
The cheap adaptations first — shade, storage, drainage, timing — ranked by cost against protection.
Disagreeing about climate with evidence and respect — the claims, the sources, and the difference between the two.
Your own electricity traced to its sources — the plants, lines and fuels behind the local socket.
Running the essentials through an outage — light, food, phones — safely and in the right order.

themes.theme: Reading a meter and a bill (EN)
themes.description: The kilowatt-hour as the unit you buy — reading your meter and reconciling it with the bill.
Finding where warmth leaves a dwelling and the sealing and insulation that pay for themselves first.
The fuels people cook with — their cost, smoke and danger — and the safest option a household can reach.

themes.theme: Sun and wind on this site (EN)
themes.description: Reading one real site for solar and wind potential — orientation, shading, exposure — before believing a brochure.
Batteries and other stores — what they hold, what they cost, and matching a store to a real need.
The energy embedded in objects and food — why making, moving and wasting things is an energy question.
The jobs that keep power flowing — lines, plants, meters — and the training routes into them locally.
Tariffs, subsidies and siting — where energy decisions are made near you and how a resident is heard.
The ranked, evidenced list of what can actually happen at your address — flood, storm, fire, slide.
One written plan a household has rehearsed — contacts, rally points, kit and the leave triggers.
Reading a building's weak points against local hazards — roof, openings, exits — and the fixes in reach.
The official warning channels where you live, tested on your own devices, and what each level demands.
Water, food, light, warmth and information for three days on your own shelf.
Re-entry done safely — structure, power, contamination — and the documentation that starts recovery.

themes.theme: Insurance and what it does not cover (RS)
themes.description: Reading a policy for the hazard exclusions, and the public help that exists where insurance does not.
Building back against the next event — elevation, materials, siting — instead of repeating the loss.
Why the same event lands unequally — age, money, mobility, location — and planning for the street, not just the house.
The event log — what happened, when, what worked — kept so the next response starts smarter.
